title: Would you use a distributed transaction here, or avoid one — and how?
summary: The senior framing of cross-service consistency — tests whether you default to avoiding distributed transactions and can justify the rare case where 2PC is actually worth its availability cost.

slides.markdown:
The expected default answer here is "avoid it" — two-phase commit (2PC) across services is a well-known availability liability, and most senior candidates are expected to reach for sagas and compensation first. The question is really testing whether you know *why* to avoid it, and whether you can name the narrow case where reaching for it anyway is defensible.

This topic walks that reasoning: why 2PC's coordinator becomes a bottleneck, when it's actually the right call, and how to answer when the business insists on "no partial state, ever."

Ask how many services are actually involved, and whether the requirement is true atomicity (all-or-nothing, visible instantly) or just eventual correctness (all-or-nothing is fine to reach a moment later, with a visible in-between state along the way).

Most "needs a transaction" requests, on inspection, actually only need eventual correctness — a customer seeing an order as "processing" for two seconds before it settles is usually fine; a customer seeing it as fully paid *and* not-yet-charged at the same instant across two screens usually isn't.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: sagas by default, 2PC only when justified
slides.markdown:
Skeleton: **default to sagas/compensation** — a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action if a later step fails — and reserve 2PC for a small, tightly-coupled, low-latency set of participants where true atomicity genuinely matters more than availability.

Saying "sagas by default" first, before being asked, is exactly the senior signal this question is probing for — it shows the avoidance is deliberate and informed, not just "I've never used 2PC."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: 2PC's blocking coordinator becomes a bottleneck
slides.markdown:
In 2PC, every participant votes "ready to commit" and then **holds its locks** while waiting for the coordinator's final decision. If the coordinator is slow, crashes, or is unreachable during that window, every participant sits blocked, holding locks, unable to serve other requests touching that data.

This is the core availability cost: 2PC doesn't just add latency, it creates a new single point where one slow or failed component (the coordinator) can stall every participant simultaneously — the opposite of what a distributed system is usually built to avoid.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the one narrow case where 2PC is defensible
slides.markdown:
2PC can be the right call for a small number of internal, co-located services (same data center, low network variance) where strict atomicity is genuinely required and the transaction is short-lived — for example, a ledger system moving money between two internal accounts that must never be observed in a half-moved state, with both accounts in the same regional cluster.

Name the specific conditions that make it defensible: few participants, low latency between them, short transaction duration, and a real (not assumed) atomicity requirement — not "it felt safer."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: estimating the lock-hold duration and throughput ceiling
slides.markdown:
A concrete estimate worth walking through out loud: if each 2PC round trip takes 20ms and every participant holds its locks for that whole duration, a single row can support at most roughly 1000ms / 20ms = 50 transactions per second before lock contention becomes the bottleneck — regardless of how many application servers you add.

Sagas don't have this ceiling in the same way, because no participant holds a lock across the whole multi-step operation — each local transaction commits and releases its lock immediately, with compensation handling the failure case instead of a held lock.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
**2PC gives real atomicity, sagas give availability — you cannot have both fully, so name which one this feature actually needs.** This is the CAP-adjacent trade-off underlying the whole question, and stating it directly is worth more than any amount of mechanism detail.

| | 2PC | Saga |
|---|---|---|
| Atomicity | True, all-or-nothing | Eventual — a visible in-between state exists |
| Availability during a slow/failed coordinator | Participants block, holding locks | Each step commits independently, no blocking |
| Failure handling | Abort and roll back | Compensating actions per completed step |

Most consumer-facing features tolerate a brief in-between state; very few need 2PC's true atomicity badly enough to accept its availability cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the business insists on "no partial state, ever"
slides.markdown:
Push back on the premise before accepting the requirement: ask for the specific user-visible harm they're trying to prevent. Often "no partial state, ever" really means "no *inconsistent* partial state that causes a wrong outcome" — which a well-designed saga with compensation already prevents, even though it does show a transient "processing" state.

If, after that conversation, the business genuinely needs true atomicity for a narrow, low-throughput internal case, that's when the 2PC conditions from earlier apply — accommodate it there, specifically, rather than reaching for 2PC system-wide to satisfy a blanket statement.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the 2PC coordinator itself crashes mid-transaction
slides.markdown:
This is 2PC's sharpest failure mode: if the coordinator crashes after participants have voted "ready" but before it records or broadcasts the final decision, every participant is stuck holding its locks indefinitely, unable to safely commit or abort on its own (each risks disagreeing with a decision the coordinator may have already made and lost).

The real answer is a recovery protocol — the coordinator persists its decision durably before crashing, and a recovering coordinator (or a designated backup) reads that log to resume exactly where it left off. Say this explicitly: 2PC without a coordinator recovery story is a design with an unaddressed failure mode, not a complete answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for 2PC as the first idea
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This touches multiple services, so I need a distributed transaction to keep them consistent."

**Why it's wrong:** reaching for 2PC first, before checking whether eventual correctness with compensation actually satisfies the requirement, trades away availability for an atomicity guarantee the feature may not even need — and introduces the blocking-coordinator failure mode as an unnecessary new risk.

**Correct model:** treat 2PC as the last resort, justified only for a small, co-located, genuinely-atomicity-requiring case — start every cross-service consistency question by asking whether a saga would actually be good enough.

"My default is a saga — a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure — because 2PC's blocking coordinator turns every participant's lock-hold time into an availability risk, and a crashed coordinator can leave the whole transaction stuck. I'd reach for 2PC only for a small number of co-located, low-latency participants where true, instantly-visible atomicity is a genuine requirement, not just a comfort. If the business says 'no partial state ever,' I'd first check whether they mean 'no wrong outcome' — which a saga already prevents — before accepting a blanket 2PC requirement."

See [distributed-transactions-and-sagas](distributed-transactions-and-sagas) for the full saga pattern and compensation mechanics this answer assumes.
